sweep_summary: Lithuanian (lith1251) is in the catalog as lexical on Senn 1966 §52; this search of works with stress in the title found nothing that contradicts it. Ten title hits: two were downloaded and read in full - Kushnir 2022 (Glossa, OA; read from a the Internet Archive HTML capture because the publisher site is bot-walled and the archived PDF is truncated) states one main accent per word placed by the strong/weak specification of morphemes with a leftmost default and the Saussurean shift to light final suffixes, confirming and refining the classification; Schmidt-Wartenberg 1897 (IF 7, archive.org) is a kymograph study of the acute/circumflex intonations and is silent on stress placement. Blevins 1993 (abstract only, JSTOR closed) and Joseph 2009 (abstract only, history of Saussure) add nothing beyond confirmation. Unread and worth acquiring: Young 1991 monograph (HathiTrust search-only, print) and Stundžia 2009 (Lithuanian textbook, no open copy) - both high; Tanaka 1974 and Kushnir 2019 dissertation (DNB print record, no Qucosa copy) - medium; Vidžiūnas 1996 (historiography) and Frings 1934 (Rhenish comparison) - low, both De Gruyter closed. Best new statement: Kushnir 2022 §2.1; it does not supersede Senn 1966 as deciding source but should be added as the modern corroborating analysis.org and the Internet Archive.

new_statements.reading: One culminative main accent per prosodic word whose position is lexically determined by the accent specifications of root and suffix (strong/weak/unaccented), with a leftmost (stem-initial) default when nothing is accented and a right-edge shift onto light 'attracting' final suffixes (the Saussurean Accent Shift); nominals fall into four accent paradigms. The acute/circumflex contrast is a contour on accented heavy syllables only and is neutralised without accent. This is a first-hand, peer-reviewed, consultant-checked modern statement that confirms the catalog's lexical coding (word domain, no weight criterion for placement) and adds an explicit default and shift rule; the author's 'pitch accent language' label belongs in tone_note.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record (Senn 1966: 'nicht an eine bestimmte Silbe gebunden', grave on short, acute/circumflex on long stressed syllables) and as Kushnir 2022 (one culminative accent, position from morpheme accent specifications, Saussurean shift); adds the explicit morpheme-valence formulation, the four accentuation classes, the mixed phonetic type, secondary-stress facts and toneme neutralisation. No contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is free (distinctive): every polysyllabic word has one stressed syllable whose position is fixed neither by syllable phonetics nor by distance from a word edge but by the accentual value of the word's morphemes (strong vs weak stems, strong vs weak endings) plus 'attractive' endings that pull stress off a preceding non-acuted syllable (the penultimate-syllable rule = de Saussure-Fortunatov law); nominals fall into four accentuation classes diagnosed by dative/accusative plural. Long stressed syllables additionally carry one of two tonemes (acute = sharp falling, circumflex = smooth rising); short stressed syllables carry stress only (grave = stress mark, not a toneme); toneme contrasts are neutralised in unstressed syllables. Stress is phonetically of a 'mixed type' (loudness, pitch, some length). Clitics are unstressed; monosyllables pattern with stressed syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §6.3: a lower-degree (secondary) stress may occur, especially in western dialects, most often on the second post-tonic syllable (mainly the penult) of a longer word (mókytojas, pùskepalis); a phonological secondary stress is possible in some rural dialects and idiolects of the standard ((tu) mýli vs (jis) mýli type pairs).
new_statements.exceptions: Some dialects restrict the freedom of stress (§6.1); toneme neutralisation in final syllables has exceptions (datives in -m(s), adverbs pusiaũ, visái, pronouns jóks, tóks, interjections, §6.9); in Samogitian dialects acute is the unmarked toneme and occurs post-tonically (§6.10); attractive endings override stem stress only after a non-acuted syllable (§2.3).
new_statements.identity_note: Standard Lithuanian (bendrinė kalba); Tanaka 1974 explicitly 'Standard Lithuanian'; Vidžiūnas 1996 concerns the East-Prussian (Lithuania Minor) written tradition of the 17th-19th c; Frings 1934 compares the Rhenish (German dialect) and Lithuanian tonal accents.

sources.citation: Mathiassen, Terje. 1996. A Short Grammar of Lithuanian. Columbus, OH: Slavica. 256 pp. (archive.org item mathiassen-short-grammar-of-lithuanian-1996, scanned text)
sources.quote: 'Word stress in Lithuanian is free in the sense that it is not bound to any specific syllable, but can vary in different forms in the declension and conjugation. It can also have distinctive value whereby stress alone can distinguish between words, cf. for instance gìria 'praises' : girià 'forest' ... Stress may be said to be morphologically distinctive in cases like gen. sg. žiemõs vs. nom. pl. žiẽmos.' p.34: 'Lithuanian can have mobile stress both in forms belonging to the nominal and the verbal system.'

sources.citation: Schmidt-Wartenberg, H. 1897. Zur Physiologie des litauischen Akzents. Indogermanische Forschungen 7: 211-223.
sources.quote: "Es ergibt sich nun als positiv gesichertes Resultat, dass die Unterscheidung von gestossenen und geschleiften Silben auch vor dem physiologischen Experiment die Probe besteht. Und zwar kann ich bestätigen, dass Brugmann mit seiner Definition des geschleiften Akzents einen glücklichen Griff gethan hat. Der geschleifte Akzent muss als ein exspiratorisch zweisilbiger [scanned; read: zweigipfliger] betrachtet werden, dessen zweiter Gipfel den ersten an Stärke etwas übertrifft." (p. 214-215) — 'It emerges as a positively secured result that the distinction between acute (gestossen) and circumflex (geschleift) syllables also passes the test of the physiological experiment ... The circumflex accent must be regarded as expiratorily two-peaked, its second peak somewhat exceeding the first in strength.'
sources.locator: IF 7 (1897) pp. 211-223; the scanned text; result statement on pp. 214-215 (scanned lines ~10960-10975)
sources.note: Read in full. An early kymograph (Rousselot apparatus) study in Chicago of one speaker from Marijampolė (plus a control from Šakiai) measuring vowel/diphthong durations and the expiratory shape of the two syllable accents (gestossen = acute, geschleift = circumflex); concludes the circumflex is two-peaked with a stronger second peak, the acute 'breaks off' sharply, no pitch data obtained, and proposes a mora count (short V = 1, long V = 2, diphthongs = 3). It says nothing about where the word accent falls; silent on the catalog's classification.

sources.quote: Crossref abstract: "In this paper I present a tonal analysis of inflection, derivation, and compounding for Standard Lithuanian nominals. I argue that nominal accents in this language surface as a result of rules of high tone insertion and high tone deletion, and that accented morphemes are represented with underlying high tones linked to the appropriate moras. The predictability of circumflex accents in stem-initial and stem-final contexts for unaccented stems is handled by invoking limited use of extraprosodicity and floating high tones."
sources.note: Standard generative treatment of the four nominal accent classes as lexical tone/accent; supports the 'lexical/paradigmatic' wording with an explicit analysis.
